query_text: first satellite compared to the latest

parts.text:
To appreciate how far space technology has advanced, we can compare the world’s very first artificial satellite, **Sputnik 1** (launched by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957), with the state-of-the-art satellites orbiting Earth today. 

Today, "the latest" satellites fall into two main categories: massive, heavy-duty **Geostationary (GEO) satellites** (such as *Jupiter 3*, the largest commercial communications satellite ever built), and smaller, mass-produced **Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites** (such as SpaceX's *Starlink V2 Mini/V3* and Amazon’s *Project Kuiper*, which operate in "mega-constellations").

---

### Side-by-Side Comparison

| Feature | The First: **Sputnik 1** (1957) | Latest Giant: **Jupiter 3** (GEO) | Latest Constellation: **Starlink V2 Mini/V3** (LEO) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Physical Size** | **Beach ball-sized:** 58 cm (22.8 in) sphere with four long antennas. | **School bus-sized:** 8 meters (26 ft) long stowed. Deployed solar arrays span **38.7 meters (127 ft)**—equivalent to a 10-story building. | **Coffee table-sized:** ~2.8 meters (9 ft) long with a single-wing solar array. |
| **Weight** | 83.6 kg (184 lbs) | **9,200 kg (20,280 lbs)** *(Over 110 times heavier than Sputnik)* | **575 to 800 kg (1,267 to 1,760 lbs)** *(7 to 10 times heavier than Sputnik)* |
| **Power Source** | Three silver-zinc batteries (No solar panels). | 14 state-of-the-art deployable solar panels generating kilowatts of power. | Integrated high-efficiency solar arrays paired with lithium-ion batteries. |
| **Technology & Payload** | Simple radio transmitter. It only broadcasted a "beep-beep" analog radio pulse. No sensors, cameras, or computers. | **Ultra-high-density broadband:** 300 steerable radio spot beams; delivers **500+ Gbps** of total data throughput to Earth. | **Laser-linked networking:** Phased-array antennas and **optical laser crosslinks** that allow satellites to beam data to each other at the speed of light. |
| **Maneuverability** | **None.** Completely passive. | Ion thrusters and chemical propellants for keeping its geostationary orbit precise. | **Autonomous ion thrusters** (argon/krypton) that automatically dodge space debris and de-orbit the satellite at end-of-life. |
| **Orbit Altitude** | LEO (Elliptical): 228 km to 947 km | Geostationary (GEO): **35,786 km (22,236 miles)** *(Stationary over the equator)* | LEO (Circular): **~550 km** |
| **Lifespan** | **3 weeks** of power; burned up in the atmosphere after **3 months**. | **15+ years** | **5 to 7 years** *(Designed for rapid upgrade cycles)* |

---

### The Major Evolutionary Leaps

#### 1. From "Beeping Ball" to Flying Supercomputer
Sputnik 1 did not collect data, take pictures, or process information. It was a technology demonstration whose sole purpose was to prove we could put something in orbit. It broadcasted on two frequencies so radio operators on Earth could track it. 
By contrast, modern satellites are **software-defined supercomputers**. They use Artificial Intelligence to route millions of internet connections simultaneously, adjust their antennas dynamically to target areas of high demand, and process vast amounts of imaging and climate data on the fly before sending it to Earth.

#### 2. Infinite Power vs. Strict Expiration Dates
Sputnik 1’s chemical batteries died after just 22 days, leaving it a silent piece of space junk until it decayed. Modern satellites rely on **advanced solar cell technology** that harvests clean energy from the sun continuously, enabling them to operate for up to 15 years in harsh radiation environments.

#### 3. Active Navigation and Collision Avoidance
Sputnik was entirely passive; once pushed into space, its path was dictated entirely by gravity and atmospheric drag. In contrast, modern LEO satellites must navigate a crowded sky. Satellites like Starlink use **ion propulsion systems** paired with autonomous tracking databases. If another object or piece of space debris gets too close, the satellite autonomously fires its thrusters to steer itself out of harm's way.

#### 4. Solitary Pioneers vs. Global Mesh Networks
For years after Sputnik, satellites were "lone wolves"—massive, expensive, and working independently. Today, the industry has shifted toward **mega-constellations**. Rather than relying on one massive satellite, companies launch thousands of smaller satellites that communicate with one another using space lasers, forming a giant, continuous mesh network wrapped around the globe to provide seamless, low-latency coverage. 

With over 10,000 active satellites now orbiting Earth, space has evolved from a silent, highly exclusive frontier into a thriving, high-speed digital highway.
